fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD sells Israel into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, and the text says "…the Israelites served him eight years." (Judges 3:8) So they're serving a king who isn't theirs, and this verse doesn't mention a quick way out. Eight years is a long time to wait on one timer.

That's it, baker. "The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years." (Judges 3:14) Earlier they served Cushan-rishathaim eight years (Judges 3:8). Eighteen is more than double that, and that's a long time to wait on a timer.

Runners aren't in this verse, friend. The text says Ehud "…blew the ram’s horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim." (Judges 3:27) Then the Israelites come down with him from the hills, and he becomes their leader.
Not quite, friend. The text says they forgot the LORD their God and "…served the Baals and the Asherahs." (Judges 3:7) Those are false gods. So they don't stop serving, they switch who they serve.

Egypt isn't in this verse, friend. The text says they "…forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs." (Judges 3:7) Those are false gods. This verse is about who they serve, not where they go.

That's the word. The LORD delivers Cushan-rishathaim into Othniel's hand, and Othniel "…prevailed against him." (Judges 3:10) Othniel is Caleb's nephew, the son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz (Judges 3:9). The Spirit of the LORD came upon him first, and then he went out to war.

Pleads is a fair guess, but it isn't the word. Israel cried out to the LORD back in verse 9. In verse 10 the LORD delivers the king into Othniel's hand, and Othniel "…prevailed against him." (Judges 3:10) That's the verb the text uses for Othniel.
That's right. The text says "…the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died." (Judges 3:11) So the rest doesn't end until Othniel dies. Forty years, friend, that's a long quiet.
Not this time. The text says the LORD gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD. So the LORD acts. Israel ends up under a foreign king again.

The tribute is already presented, and Ehud has ushered out the men who carried it (Judges 3:18). What he says instead is, "I have a secret message for you, O king." (Judges 3:19) Then the king says, "Silence," and all his attendants leave him.

Peace isn't what Ehud says, friend. The text has him say, "I have a secret message for you, O king." (Judges 3:19) The king answers, "Silence," and all his attendants leave him. Then it's just the two of them.
Guarding isn't the word. The text says Ehud went out "…closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him." (Judges 3:23) Locked doors are what the servants run into in the next verse.

Marking isn't the word, friend. The text says Ehud went out "…closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him." (Judges 3:23) Locked doors are what the servants find in the next verse. I've locked a door behind me too, usually with my keys inside.

Resting is a sensible guess, but it isn't what they say. The text has them say, "He must be relieving himself in the cool room…" (Judges 3:24) They find the doors locked and that's the guess they make. Then they wait until they become worried (Judges 3:25).

A meeting isn't what they say, friend. The text has them say, "He must be relieving himself in the cool room…" (Judges 3:24) That's their guess when they find the doors locked. A meeting never comes up in the verse.

You're thinking of Samson, who struck down a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone (Judges 15:15). He was a judge of Israel too (Judges 15:20). Shamgar's tool is different, friend. The text says he struck down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad. (Judges 3:31)
